source.title: Scaling depth capacity via zero/one-layer model expansion

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It fits validation-loss scaling curves against compute for progressive-training variants and fixed-size training, providing a conceptual test of compute-scaling behavior with a different training setup from the original scaling-law studies.
record.gate_note: Figure 2 reports fitted validation-loss scaling laws against compute for LLAMA3 and DeepSeekV3 progressive-training variants and fixed-size baselines. Other reported expansion, initialization, and schedule comparisons do not directly test the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: Figure 2 fits validation loss as a power law of compute (with an irreducible term) for fixed-size and progressive-training LLAMA3 (dense) and DeepSeekV3 (MoE) pretraining runs. These fits bear on V1 within a narrow range and on V7, since the exponents change with the training regime and model family.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors say zero/one-layer progressive training has a better scaling exponent than fixed-size training and gives 3 to 5x compute efficiency. The growing advantage at larger scale is partly read off extrapolated fitted curves rather than measured runs.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses zero/one-layer depth expansion during pretraining, rather than the standard fixed-size scaling-law setup; it compares progressive runs with fixed-size baselines.
record.method_sensitivity: The fitted compute exponents differ across progressive and fixed-size training. The paper also reports differences across initialization variants, but does not state that these differences alter the exponent in a general way.
record.problems: The Figure 2 fits cover only the reported LLAMA3 and DeepSeekV3 size ranges and training setup. The text provides fit R² values but no error bars or confidence intervals for the fitted parameters.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows were omitted for the tested versions. Loss and compute comparisons elsewhere in the paper concern depth-expansion effectiveness or training choices, not the listed scaling-law versions.

untested.parts: Separate scaling in parameters or in tokens. Scaling over several orders of magnitude: the measured runs span roughly 2e19 to 1e21 FLOPs (about 0.25B to 2B parameters at 50 tokens per parameter), and far less for DeepSeekV3.
No larger runs are trained to check the fitted curves. The extrapolated speedups are not validated.
Compute-optimal allocation is not studied; the tokens-per-parameter ratio is fixed.
ResNet/ImageNet runs exist but no scaling-law fits are reported for them.
Sensitivity to parameter counting or fitting method is not tested, and curvature away from a power law is not examined.

missing.what: Figure 2 annotates speedups (3.3x to 5.9x) at compute levels up to about 1e23 FLOPs, beyond the trained sizes. The claim of an 'increasing advantage at larger scales' rests on extrapolating the fitted curves, with no validation run.
Individual run losses and compute values behind the fits are not tabulated. Only the fitted equations and R² are given, so readers cannot check residual curvature.

record.verdict_notes: This is primarily a training-efficiency paper. Scaling-law evidence is limited to Figure 2. Each family's fits share a single irreducible loss (2.373, 2.022), a fitting choice that constrains the exponent comparison. No uncertainty is given on the exponents, so the differences (about 0.02 to 0.03) lack confidence intervals. Compute for progressive runs is total FLOPs, including the small-model phase.

versions.untested_parts: Tests loss scaling against compute in the reported progressive-training and fixed-size runs. It does not separately vary parameters or tokens while holding the other quantities non-bottlenecking, or establish those individual scaling relationships.
The study does not report predictions of much larger runs made from power-law fits to smaller runs.
It compares training approaches at different compute costs, but does not determine loss-minimising parameter and token allocations as functions of a fixed compute budget.
It does not compare depth, width, or architecture details at a fixed parameter count to test their effect on loss.
No other modality or training regime of the types named in this version is tested.
The reported outcomes are validation loss, not downstream-task performance.

The study shows different fitted compute exponents across progressive and fixed-size training setups. It does not test sensitivity to parameter-counting or fitting choices, compute-optimal allocation, or systematic bending of curves away from a power law.
